title: PINN Ecosystem
description: A layered taxonomy of the coupled choices, extensions, evaluation practices, infrastructure, and scientific contexts that define a physics-informed neural network workflow.

governance.evidencePolicy: Community additions are proposals. They enter the curated taxonomy only after evidence review.

layers.title: Problem & Physics
layers.description: Defines the governing relations, numerical character, observations, and physical context that drive every downstream choice.

layers.title: PINN Purpose
layers.description: States what the model must accomplish: solve, infer, discover, reuse, quantify, optimize, or control.

layers.title: Representation
layers.description: Chooses how inputs, outputs, bases, architectures, and activations represent the physical state.

layers.title: Physics Enforcement
layers.description: Specifies which physical conditions are imposed, how they are encoded, and how competing objectives are balanced.

layers.title: Numerical Evaluation of Physics
layers.description: Evaluates differential, integral, discrete, or time-stepping operators used to construct the physical residual.

layers.title: Training
layers.description: Controls collocation, optimization, initialization, scaling, stabilization, schedules, and staged learning.

layers.title: Structural Extensions
layers.description: Adds decomposition, operator learning, reduced models, probabilistic methods, numerical hybrids, reuse, and parallel execution.

layers.title: Evaluation & Reliability
layers.description: Tests numerical accuracy, physical fidelity, robustness, uncertainty, computational cost, theory, and failure modes.

layers.title: Ecosystem
layers.description: Connects implementation software, reporting standards, reproducibility, and scientific application domains.

groups.title: Problem / Physical-System Definition
groups.description: This is the level before the neural network itself. It determines nearly every downstream choice.

groups.title: Computational Role / PINN Task
groups.description: This is another major branch that should probably appear near the center of the final figure.

groups.title: Input Representation
groups.description: This is a true PINN element.

groups.title: Output / State Representation
groups.description: Another fundamental PINN element.

groups.title: Neural Architecture / Approximation Model
groups.description: This is what people usually think of first when they say “PINN architecture,” but it is only one branch.

groups.title: Network Hyperparameters
groups.description: This should be a subordinate branch under architecture.

groups.title: Activation Function
groups.description: Definitely one of the major PINN elements.

groups.title: Physics-Enforcement Mechanism
groups.description: This deserves a major branch of its own.

groups.title: Physical Constraints
groups.description: Separate this from the mechanism used to enforce them.

groups.title: Loss Function / Objective Construction
groups.description: Another central branch.

groups.title: Loss Weighting / Balancing
groups.description: This should not be merged with the loss itself.

groups.title: Differentiation / Differential-Operator Evaluation
groups.description: Another major PINN element.

groups.title: Collocation / Sampling
groups.description: Your example of sampler should become this entire branch.

groups.title: Optimizer
groups.description: A major branch.

groups.title: Learning-Rate Strategy
groups.description: This should be distinct from the optimizer.

groups.title: Initialization
groups.description: Another genuine PINN training element.

groups.title: Scaling / Normalization / Preprocessing
groups.description: Often neglected, but your manuscript correctly treats it as part of the formulation.

groups.title: Regularization / Training Stabilization
groups.description: Controls collocation, optimization, initialization, scaling, stabilization, schedules, and staged learning.

groups.title: Training Strategy
groups.description: This is larger than the optimizer.

groups.title: Decomposition
groups.description: This is exactly the type of “related approach” that should appear in the general PINN map.

subgroups.title: Named/general variants appearing in the manuscript

groups.title: Operator Learning
groups.description: I would make this a separate neighboring branch rather than place it simply under “architecture.”

groups.title: Reduced-Order / Basis Approaches
groups.description: Closely related but not identical to operator learning.

groups.title: Hybrid Numerical–PINN Methods
groups.description: This is another essential branch for the “general view.”

groups.title: Data
groups.description: Data should also appear in the general figure.

groups.title: Inverse Problems and Discovery
groups.description: Although these are computational roles, they deserve a visible methodological branch.

groups.title: Uncertainty Quantification / Probabilistic PINNs
groups.description: A major neighboring family.

groups.title: Generalization / Knowledge Reuse
groups.description: Adds decomposition, operator learning, reduced models, probabilistic methods, numerical hybrids, reuse, and parallel execution.

groups.title: Parallelization / Computational Execution
groups.description: Also related to the PINN ecosystem.

groups.title: Evaluation
groups.description: This should be a major outer layer of the diagram, not an afterthought.

groups.title: Validation / Benchmarking
groups.description: Distinct from metric calculation.

groups.title: Theory
groups.description: This belongs in the ecosystem even though it is not a PINN “setting.”

groups.title: Software / Framework / Infrastructure
groups.description: A final ecosystem diagram should definitely include this.

subgroups.title: PINN/scientific-ML software appearing in the manuscript

groups.title: Reproducibility / Reporting
groups.description: This should probably appear in the outermost ring.

groups.title: Failure Modes / Challenges
groups.description: This is very important because each development can later be visually connected to the challenge it tries to solve.

groups.title: Application / Scientific Domain
groups.description: This can form the outermost contextual layer.

relations.summary: The physical system constrains the useful computational role.
Coordinates, parameters, geometry, and conditions follow from the problem definition.
State variables and auxiliary outputs must expose the quantities required by the physics.
Problem regularity and geometry affect whether physics is imposed softly, weakly, or exactly.
Operator order and structure select a suitable differentiation pathway.
Localized, stiff, multiscale, or irregular behavior changes the sampling strategy.
Large, long-time, or multiphysics systems often motivate decomposition.
Problem characteristics determine the most likely numerical failure modes.
Observed variables and parameter fields enter through the input representation.
Data availability and quality determine which mismatch terms are defensible.
Inverse recovery and discovery require informative observations.
Independent data enable validation beyond the training objective.
The computational purpose decides whether inputs are coordinates, parameters, functions, or observations.
Forward, inverse, discovery, and control tasks require different outputs.
The role helps select a pointwise network, sequence model, graph model, or operator.
Evaluation criteria must reflect the intended computational role.
Inverse and discovery tasks expose parameters, coefficients, or latent states as outputs.
Identifiability depends on a suitable combination of physics and data objectives.
Inverse conclusions require stability and identifiability analysis.
The approximation model consumes the chosen coordinates, parameters, fields, or functions.
Primitive, mixed, and auxiliary-output formulations change derivative order and cost.
Predicted states and auxiliary variables determine the available residual terms.
Depth, width, topology, and parameter sharing configure the architecture.
Activation choice controls smoothness, frequency representation, and gradient propagation.
Initialization acts on the selected architecture and basis.
Model topology affects parallel and distributed execution.
The activation must provide the derivative smoothness required by the operator.
An enforcement mechanism acts on explicit physical constraints.
Soft, weak, variational, hard, or discrete enforcement changes the objective.
Strong-form residuals and alternative formulations evaluate physics differently.
Equations, boundary conditions, interfaces, and admissibility become objective terms or exact constructions.
Boundary, initial, interface, and observation constraints require dedicated point sets.
Composite objectives require explicit or adaptive weighting.
The objective landscape determines optimizer behavior.
Loss balancing changes gradient scales seen by the optimizer.
Differential and numerical operators generate the physics residual.
Derivative evaluation often dominates memory and parallelization requirements.
Collocation and data points define where every objective term is evaluated.
Adaptive resampling and causal point selection are part of the training schedule.
Each optimizer depends on a compatible learning-rate policy or line search.
Staged training can switch optimizers and batch policies.
Initialization influences the region of the loss landscape reached by optimization.
Nondimensionalization and residual scaling change objective conditioning.
Well-scaled inputs and outputs improve optimizer conditioning.
Regularization, clipping, stopping, and restarts modify the training process.
Decomposition replaces one global model with coupled local networks.
Subdomains introduce interface and transmission conditions.
Each subdomain or time window needs its own collocation design.
Independent subnetworks create domain-parallel execution opportunities.
Operator learning consumes functions, fields, or sensor samples rather than coordinates alone.
Branch-trunk, Fourier, graph, or wavelet operators alter the approximation model.
Learning a function-to-function map enables reuse across conditions and parameters.
Reduced bases and low-rank representations constrain the model space.
Reduced representations can be embedded in classical solver hybrids.
Numerical solvers and discrete operators provide alternative physics-enforcement pathways.
Classical discretizations can replace or complement automatic differentiation.
Hybrid workflows require interoperable neural and numerical software.
Probabilistic PINNs add Bayesian, generative, ensemble, or invertible representations.
Likelihoods, priors, and adversarial terms modify the objective.
Uncertainty predictions require coverage, calibration, and reliability evaluation.
Reuse claims require interpolation, extrapolation, and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
Distributed execution depends on GPU, HPC, and framework infrastructure.
Metrics become evidence only through appropriate benchmarks and comparisons.
Benchmark conclusions require complete, reproducible configuration reporting.
Spectral bias and smoothness theory inform activation selection.
Error, stability, NTK, Hessian, and conditioning analyses study the objective.
Loss-landscape and curvature analyses guide optimizer choice.
Stabilization methods respond to optimization and approximation failures.
Decomposition targets scale, locality, and long-time failures.
Reliability metrics should expose known numerical and physical pathologies.
Frameworks and infrastructure determine which configurations can be reproduced.
Complete reporting lets readers reproduce numerical and physical evaluation.
The scientific domain supplies the equations, scales, geometry, and admissibility requirements.

builder.title: PINN Design Studio
builder.description: Select compatible elements, inspect design warnings, and generate a portable architecture diagram.

stages.title: Problem & purpose
stages.description: Define the physical system, task, and data regime.

stages.title: Representation
stages.description: Choose model inputs, outputs, architecture, and activation.

stages.title: Physics construction
stages.description: Select the imposed physics, enforcement route, and objective.

stages.title: Numerical evaluation
stages.description: Decide how the residual is differentiated and where it is evaluated.

stages.title: Training
stages.description: Configure optimization, scaling, initialization, and stabilization.

stages.title: Structural extensions
stages.description: Add only the neighboring methods required by the problem.

stages.title: Verification & reporting
stages.description: Specify how the design will be tested, implemented, and reproduced.
